title: Integers and Operations
notes: Integers are whole numbers including negative numbers, zero, and positive numbers (e.g., -3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3). On a number line, numbers to the right are greater than those to the left. Operations: Adding two positive integers yields a positive; adding two negative yields a negative. Adding a positive and negative requires subtraction of their absolute values, taking the sign of the larger absolute value. Multiplying two integers with the same sign yields a positive; different signs yield a negative. BODMAS/PEMDAS rules apply for order of operations.
subject: Mathematics
author: CBC Kenya Team

title: Fractions, Decimals, and Percentages
notes: A fraction represents part of a whole (numerator/denominator). Proper fractions have a numerator smaller than the denominator; improper fractions have a larger numerator. Decimals are fractions with denominators of 10, 100, 1000, etc. Percentages are fractions with a denominator of 100. Conversions: To convert a fraction to a decimal, divide numerator by denominator; to decimal to percentage, multiply by 100. Kenyan currency (Shillings and Cents) provides real-life applications for decimals.
subject: Mathematics
author: CBC Kenya Team

title: Algebraic Expressions
notes: Algebra involves using letters (variables) to represent unknown values. A term is a number, variable, or product (e.g., 4x). Like terms have the same variable power (e.g., 3x and 5x). Simplifying expressions involves combining like terms through addition or subtraction. Expanding brackets: a(b + c) = ab + ac. Factorization is the reverse: ab + ac = a(b + c). Substitution involves replacing variables with given numerical values to evaluate the expression.
subject: Mathematics
author: CBC Kenya Team

title: Linear Equations in One Unknown
notes: A linear equation forms a straight line when graphed and has one unknown (e.g., 2x + 3 = 7). Solving involves isolating the variable (x) on one side of the equals sign. Use inverse operations: if the equation adds a number, subtract it from both sides; if it multiplies, divide both sides. Always perform the same operation on both sides to maintain balance. Forming equations from word problems is a key competency in the Kenyan CBC syllabus.
subject: Mathematics
author: CBC Kenya Team

title: Geometry: Angles and Polygons
notes: Angles are measured in degrees. Types: acute (<90°), right (=90°), obtuse (>90° and <180°), reflex (>180°). Angles on a straight line add up to 180°; angles at a point add up to 360°. Vertically opposite angles are equal. A polygon is a closed 2D shape with straight sides. The sum of interior angles of an n-sided polygon is (2n - 4) × 90° or (n - 2) × 180°. A regular polygon has equal sides and equal angles.
subject: Mathematics
author: CBC Kenya Team

title: Ratios, Rates, and Proportions
notes: A ratio compares two or more quantities of the same kind (e.g., 2:3). A rate compares quantities of different kinds (e.g., speed in km/h, exchange rate of KES to USD). Direct proportion: as one quantity increases, the other increases at the same rate (y = kx). Inverse proportion: as one increases, the other decreases (y = k/x). Unitary method: find the value of one unit first, then multiply to find the required value.
subject: Mathematics
author: CBC Kenya Team

title: Linear Inequalities
notes: Inequalities use symbols < (less than), > (greater than), ≤ (less than or equal to), and ≥ (greater than or equal to). Solving inequalities is similar to solving equations: isolate the unknown using inverse operations. CRITICAL RULE: When multiplying or dividing both sides by a negative number, reverse the inequality sign. Representing solutions on a number line: an open circle (○) is used for < and >; a closed circle (●) for ≤ and ≥.
subject: Mathematics
author: CBC Kenya Team

title: Sets and Venn Diagrams
notes: A set is a well-defined collection of objects/elements. Notation: {} or ∅ for an empty set. Universal set (ξ) contains all elements under consideration. Subset: A is a subset of B if all elements of A are in B. Intersection (A ∩ B) contains elements common to both sets. Union (A ∪ B) contains all elements in A or B or both. Venn diagrams use overlapping circles to visually represent sets and solve real-life problems involving groupings.
subject: Mathematics
author: CBC Kenya Team

title: Measurements: Area and Volume
notes: Area is the amount of space covered by a 2D shape. Area of a trapezium = ½(a + b)h. Area of a circle = πr². Area of a sector = (θ/360) × πr². Volume is the space occupied by a 3D object. Volume of a prism = base area × height. Volume of a cylinder = πr²h. Capacity is the volume of liquid a container can hold, measured in litres (1 m³ = 1000 litres). Connecting volume to capacity is essential for practical CBC tasks.
subject: Mathematics
author: CBC Kenya Team

title: Matrices and Transformations
notes: A matrix is a rectangular arrangement of numbers in rows and columns. Order of a matrix is given as rows × columns. Addition and subtraction of matrices is done element by element, but matrices must be of the same order. Scalar multiplication involves multiplying every element by a constant. Transformation matrices can represent reflections, rotations, and enlargements on the Cartesian plane, mapping object points to image points.
subject: Mathematics
author: CBC Kenya Team

title: Quadratic Equations and Expressions
notes: A quadratic expression is of the form ax² + bx + c. Expanding brackets: (x + a)(x + b) = x² + (a+b)x + ab. Factorising is the reverse: finding two numbers that multiply to give 'c' and add to give 'b'. A quadratic equation (ax² + bx + c = 0) can be solved by factorisation: set each bracket to zero and solve for x. The solutions are the roots where the parabola crosses the x-axis. The quadratic formula x = (-b ± √(b²-4ac)) / 2a is used for harder equations.
subject: Mathematics
author: CBC Kenya Team

title: Simultaneous Equations
notes: Simultaneous equations involve two unknowns (x and y) solved together. Methods: 1) Substitution: rearrange one equation to make x or y the subject, then substitute into the other. 2) Elimination: multiply equations so coefficients of one variable match, then add or subtract to eliminate it. Real-life applications include finding costs of items (e.g., prices of maize and beans in a Kenyan market) when given combined purchase totals.
subject: Mathematics
author: CBC Kenya Team

title: Trigonometry: Sine, Cosine, Tangent
notes: Trigonometry deals with relationships between sides and angles in right-angled triangles. SOH CAH TOA: Sin θ = Opposite/Hypotenuse, Cos θ = Adjacent/Hypotenuse, Tan θ = Opposite/Adjacent. Used to find missing sides or angles. Inverse trig functions (sin⁻¹, cos⁻¹, tan⁻¹) find the angle. Trigonometric ratios are vital in surveying, navigation, and engineering in Kenya, such as determining the height of buildings or slopes of roads.
subject: Mathematics
author: CBC Kenya Team

title: Scale Drawing and Bearings
notes: A scale drawing represents an object or distance at a reduced or enlarged size. Scale = drawing length : actual length. Used in maps and building plans. Bearings indicate direction: measured from North in a clockwise direction, written as 3-figure digits (e.g., 045°, 270°). The bearing of B from A is the angle at A. Back bearing = Forward bearing ± 180°. Compass directions (N, S, E, W) and angles of elevation/depression are applied.
subject: Mathematics
author: CBC Kenya Team

title: Data Handling and Probability
notes: Data can be discrete (counted) or continuous (measured). Mean = sum of values / count. Median is the middle value; Mode is the most frequent. Grouped data uses class intervals and midpoints. Probability of an event P(E) = Number of favorable outcomes / Total outcomes. Ranges from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain). P(not E) = 1 - P(E). Combined events: mutually exclusive (P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B)), independent (P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B)).
subject: Mathematics
author: CBC Kenya Team

title: Oral Literature and Narratives
notes: Oral literature is transmitted by word of mouth and includes narratives, songs, riddles, and proverbs. Narratives are classified into: a) Myths (explain origins of natural phenomena), b) Legends (historical heroes/events, e.g., Wangu wa Makeri), c) Trickster tales (clever character outwitting stronger ones, e.g., Hare and Hyena), d) Dilemma tales (pose a moral choice). Oral performance requires audience participation, making it dynamic and contextual to Kenyan communities.
subject: English
author: CBC Kenya Team

title: Narrative and Descriptive Writing
notes: Narrative writing tells a story with a plot, characters, setting, and climax. Use past tenses and time transitions (e.g., subsequently, eventually). Descriptive writing paints a picture using words. Focus on the five senses: sight, sound, smell, touch, taste. Use figurative language (similes, metaphors) and strong adjectives. 'Show, don't tell' is key: instead of 'he was angry', write 'his fists clenched and veins bulged'. CBC emphasizes creativity and personal expression.
subject: English
author: CBC Kenya Team

title: Reading Comprehension and Inference
notes: Comprehension involves understanding explicit text (directly stated) and implicit text (reading between the lines). Inference requires using context clues and prior knowledge to deduce meanings. Skimming is reading quickly for the gist; scanning is looking for specific details. When answering comprehension questions, use the PEEL method: Point, Evidence (quote), Explain, Link. Vocabulary in context: use surrounding words to guess unfamiliar Kenyan idioms or terms.
subject: English
author: CBC Kenya Team

title: Grammar: Tenses and Parts of Speech
notes: Parts of speech: Nouns (naming words), Pronouns (replace nouns), Verbs (action/state), Adjectives (describe nouns), Adverbs (describe verbs), Prepositions (show relationship), Conjunctions (join clauses), Interjections. Tenses indicate time: Present (habitual actions), Past (completed actions), Future (will happen). Continuous tenses show ongoing action (is/was + -ing). Perfect tenses show completed actions with present relevance (has/had + past participle). Subject-verb agreement is crucial.
subject: English
author: CBC Kenya Team

title: Poetry Appreciation
notes: Poetry uses rhythmic and aesthetic qualities of language to convey meaning. Form: stanza structure, rhyme scheme, rhythm. Oral poetry in Kenya includes work songs, dirges, and praise poetry. Written poetry uses literary devices: Simile (comparison using 'like'/'as'), Metaphor (direct comparison), Personification (human qualities to non-human), Alliteration (repetition of initial consonant sounds). Tone is the poet's attitude; Mood is the feeling evoked in the reader.
subject: English
author: CBC Kenya Team

title: Expository and Informative Writing
notes: Expository writing explains, informs, or describes. It is factual and objective, avoiding personal opinions. Types: process essays (how to do something, e.g., making ugali), cause and effect, compare and contrast. Structure: Introduction with thesis statement, body paragraphs with facts/evidence, conclusion summarizing main points. Use transitional words for coherence (furthermore, in addition, consequently). Research and note-making are essential pre-writing skills.
subject: English
author: CBC Kenya Team

title: Literature: Character and Plot Analysis
notes: Analyzing set texts (novels, plays, short stories) is core to the Kenyan syllabus. Characters: Protagonist (main), Antagonist (opposes main), Dynamic (changes), Static (unchanging). Characterization through dialogue, action, and description. Plot: the sequence of events. Structure: Exposition, Rising action, Climax, Turning point, Falling action, Resolution/Denouement. Conflicts can be internal (man vs self) or external (man vs man, man vs society).
subject: English
author: CBC Kenya Team

title: Figurative Language and Sound Devices
notes: Figurative language deviates from literal meaning for special effect. Metonymy (substituting the name of an attribute for the thing itself, e.g., 'The crown' for royalty). Synecdoche (part represents whole). Irony: Situational (opposite of expected happens), Verbal (saying opposite of meaning), Dramatic (audience knows what characters don't). Sound devices: Assonance (repetition of vowel sounds), Consonance (repetition of consonant sounds), Onomatopoeia (words that imitate sounds, e.g., buzz).
subject: English
author: CBC Kenya Team

title: Formal Writing: Letters and Emails
notes: Formal writing has a professional tone, avoids slang/abbreviations, and uses complex sentences. Formal letters: Sender's address, Date, Receiver's address, Salutation (Dear Sir/Madam), Subject line, Body (introduction, main content, conclusion), Complimentary close (Yours faithfully). Emails: To, CC, BCC, Subject, formal salutation. Used for job applications, complaining to county offices, or requesting information. Layout and formatting marks are strictly graded.
subject: English
author: CBC Kenya Team

title: Direct and Indirect Speech
notes: Direct speech quotes exact words using quotation marks: He said, 'I am going home.' Indirect speech reports what was said without quotes: He said that he was going home. Rules for conversion: Remove commas/quotes, add 'that'. Change pronouns (I -> he/she). Change tenses (Present -> Past, Past -> Past Perfect). Change time/place references (today -> that day, here -> there, tomorrow -> the next day). Questions become statements; commands use 'to' + infinitive.
subject: English
author: CBC Kenya Team

title: Argumentative and Persuasive Writing
notes: Argumentative writing presents a stance on a debatable issue (e.g., 'Should school uniforms be mandatory?'). Structure: Introduction with a hook and thesis, Body paragraphs with claims supported by evidence (facts, statistics, expert opinion), Counter-argument (acknowledge opposing view) and Rebuttal (prove it wrong), Conclusion. Persuasive techniques (AFOREST): Alliteration, Facts, Opinions, Rhetorical questions, Emotive language, Statistics, Rule of three. Tone is confident and formal.
subject: English
author: CBC Kenya Team

title: Poetry Analysis: Themes and Stylistics
notes: Deep analysis of set poems. Theme: the central idea (e.g., corruption, betrayal, cultural conflict). Stylistic devices are the tools the poet uses. Enjambment: continuation of a line without pause, creating flow or urgency. Caesura: a pause within a line, often marked by punctuation. Symbolism: using objects to represent abstract ideas. Allegory: a narrative with a hidden meaning. Evaluate effectiveness: how do the devices enhance the theme? Always embed quotes in PEEL paragraphs.
subject: English
author: CBC Kenya Team

title: Literature: Themes and Societal Issues
notes: Kenyan set texts often explore socio-economic and political themes. Common themes: Impact of colonialism, rural-urban migration, poverty and wealth disparity, corruption and bad governance, HIV/AIDS, cultural erosion vs tradition, and gender roles. Analyzing themes requires linking characters' experiences to broader societal contexts. Relate text to context: how does the author's background or historical period influence the message? Use specific textual references to substantiate points.
subject: English
author: CBC Kenya Team

title: Report and Minutes Writing
notes: Reports present findings of an investigation or survey. Structure: Title, Terms of Reference (why written), Procedure/Methodology (how data was collected), Findings (the facts, often bulleted), Conclusions (inferences from findings), Recommendations (suggested actions, numbered). Written in formal, impersonal language (passive voice). Minutes: official record of a meeting. Include: Date, time, venue, present/absent members, matters arising, AOB, date of next meeting.
subject: English
author: CBC Kenya Team

title: Note Making and Summary Writing
notes: Note making extracts key points from a text, omitting illustrations and repetitions. Use abbreviations, symbols, and numbered lists/bullet points. Must be concise but retain core meaning. Summary writing condenses a passage to a specific word count (e.g., 'In about 80 words...'). Steps: Read for main ideas, underline key points, draft summary in own words, edit to meet word count. Paraphrasing is essential: replace complex vocabulary with simpler synonyms without losing meaning.
subject: English
author: CBC Kenya Team

title: Scientific Investigation and Laboratory Safety
notes: Integrated Science begins with the scientific method: Observation, Hypothesis, Experiment, Analysis, Conclusion. Variables: Independent (changed), Dependent (measured), Control (kept constant). Laboratory safety rules: No eating/drinking, wear protective gear (goggles, lab coat), know location of fire extinguisher and first aid kit. Hazard symbols warn of toxic, flammable, corrosive, or irritant substances. First aid for acid spills involves washing with plenty of water.
subject: Science
author: CBC Kenya Team

title: Matter and Its Properties
notes: Matter is anything that occupies space and has mass. States: Solid (fixed shape/volume), Liquid (fixed volume, takes container shape), Gas (fills container). Changes of state: Melting (solid to liquid), Boiling (liquid to gas), Condensation (gas to liquid), Freezing (liquid to solid), Sublimation (solid directly to gas, e.g., iodine). Mixtures: Components can be separated by physical methods (filtration, distillation, evaporation). Pure substances (elements/compounds) cannot.
subject: Science
author: CBC Kenya Team

title: Force and Energy
notes: A force is a push or a pull. Measured in Newtons (N). Types: Gravitational (weight = mass × 10 N/kg), Friction (opposes motion), Magnetic, Electrostatic. Balanced forces = no change in motion (constant speed or stationary). Unbalanced forces = acceleration/deceleration. Energy is the capacity to do work. Kinetic energy (movement), Potential energy (stored position). Energy transfers occur constantly; the total energy is conserved (cannot be created or destroyed).
subject: Science
author: CBC Kenya Team

title: Cells and Human Body Systems
notes: Cells are the basic unit of life. Plant cells have cell wall, chloroplasts, and large vacuole; animal cells do not. Organs form systems. Digestive system: breaks down food (alimentary canal from mouth to anus). Absorption occurs in the small intestine (villi increase surface area). Circulatory system: heart pumps blood via arteries, veins, and capillaries. Respiratory system: lungs facilitate gaseous exchange (alveoli). Kenya's CBC emphasizes applying health knowledge to prevent local diseases.
subject: Science
author: CBC Kenya Team

title: Earth and Environment
notes: The Earth consists of crust, mantle, and core. The atmosphere (troposphere, stratosphere) supports life and weather. Weather elements: temperature, rainfall, humidity, wind, atmospheric pressure. Measured using thermometer, rain gauge, hygrometer, wind vane, barometer. Soil is formed by weathering of rocks. Types: sandy, clay, loamy. Soil conservation prevents erosion (terracing, afforestation, contour plowing)—vital for Kenya's agricultural economy. Water pollution (industrial, agricultural) affects water tables.
subject: Science
author: CBC Kenya Team

title: Chemical Reactions and Word Equations
notes: A chemical reaction changes reactants into new products. Signs: color change, gas evolved, precipitate formed, temperature change. Types: Combination (A + B → AB), Decomposition (AB → A + B), Displacement (A + BC → AC + B). Word equations represent reactions (e.g., Carbon + Oxygen → Carbon dioxide). Catalysis: substances that speed up reactions without being used up (e.g., enzymes in biological washing powders). Conservation of mass: total mass of reactants equals total mass of products.
subject: Science
author: CBC Kenya Team

title: Electricity and Magnetism
notes: Static electricity is caused by friction transferring electrons. Like charges repel, unlike charges attract. Current electricity is the flow of electrons through a conductor. Measured in Amperes (A). Voltage (V) is the driving force; Resistance (Ω) opposes flow. Ohm's Law: V = IR. Series circuits: same current, voltage divides. Parallel circuits: same voltage, current divides. Magnets have North and South poles. Electromagnets are made by passing current through a coil of wire (solenoid).
subject: Science
author: CBC Kenya Team

title: Human Reproduction and Health
notes: Reproduction ensures continuity of life. Male system: testes produce sperm, testosterone. Female system: ovaries produce ova, estrogen/progesterone; uterus hosts fetus. Fertilization: sperm meets ovum in fallopian tube. Menstrual cycle: 28-day cycle preparing uterus for pregnancy. Adolescence: physical and emotional changes due to hormones. STIs and HIV/AIDS: transmission, prevention (ABC approach: Abstinence, Being faithful, Condom use), and impact on Kenyan youth.
subject: Science
author: CBC Kenya Team

title: Ecology and Ecosystems
notes: Ecology studies interactions between organisms and their environment. Producers (plants) make food via photosynthesis. Consumers (animals) eat food. Decomposers (bacteria/fungi) break down dead matter. Food chains show energy flow; food webs show interconnected chains. Carbon cycle: CO2 absorbed by plants, released by respiration, combustion, and decay. Human activities (deforestation, burning fossil fuels) increase greenhouse gases, causing global warming and climate change impacts in Kenya.
subject: Science
author: CBC Kenya Team

title: Light and Sound Waves
notes: Light travels in straight lines (rectilinear propagation). Reflection: light bounces off surfaces. Law: angle of incidence = angle of reflection. Refraction: light bends when passing between media of different densities. Lenses (convex/concave) refract light to form images. Sound is a longitudinal wave requiring a medium. Properties: Pitch (frequency), Loudness (amplitude). Echoes are reflected sound. Speed of sound is approx 340 m/s in air; light is much faster (3 × 10⁸ m/s).
subject: Science
author: CBC Kenya Team

title: Chemistry: Atomic Structure and Bonding
notes: Atoms are the smallest particles of elements. Structure: Protons (+ve, in nucleus), Neutrons (neutral, nucleus), Electrons (-ve, shells). Atomic number = protons; Mass number = protons + neutrons. Isotopes: same atomic number, different mass number. Electron configurations determine chemical properties. Bonding: Ionic (transfer of electrons, e.g., NaCl). Covalent (sharing of electrons, e.g., H₂O). Metallic bonding (sea of delocalized electrons).
subject: Science
author: CBC Kenya Team

title: Physics: Forces and Pressure
notes: Force changes shape, speed, or direction. Weight = mass × gravity (W = mg). Turning effect (moment) = Force × perpendicular distance from pivot. Principle of moments: clockwise moment = anticlockwise moment (equilibrium). Pressure = Force / Area. Measured in Pascals (Pa). Applications: Sharp knife cuts easily (small area, high pressure). Atmospheric pressure supports liquid columns. Pressure in liquids increases with depth: P = hρg (h=depth, ρ=density, g=gravity).
subject: Science
author: CBC Kenya Team

title: Biology: Nutrition and Plant Physiology
notes: Nutrition is the process of obtaining and utilizing food. Autotrophic (plants): Photosynthesis (6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂) using chlorophyll and sunlight. Factors affecting rate: light intensity, CO₂ concentration, temperature. Heterotrophic (animals): Holozoic nutrition (ingestion, digestion, absorption, assimilation, egestion). Plant transport: Xylem carries water/minerals (transpiration pull); Phloem transports manufactured food (translocation). Important for Kenyan agriculture and food security.
subject: Science
author: CBC Kenya Team

title: Physics: Linear Motion
notes: Motion is a change in position. Distance is scalar (magnitude only); Displacement is vector (magnitude + direction). Speed = Distance / Time. Velocity = Displacement / Time. Acceleration = (Final Velocity - Initial Velocity) / Time. Equations of linear motion (v = u + at, s = ut + ½at², v² = u² + 2as). Ticker-timers measure motion in the lab. Free fall: acceleration due to gravity (g ≈ 10 m/s²). Air resistance opposes motion, leading to terminal velocity.
subject: Science
author: CBC Kenya Team

title: Chemistry: Acids, Bases, and Salts
notes: Acids turn blue litmus red, taste sour (H⁺ ions). Bases turn red litmus blue, feel soapy (OH⁻ ions). Alkalis are soluble bases. pH scale: 0-6 (acidic), 7 (neutral), 8-14 (alkaline). Indicators: litmus, phenolphthalein, universal indicator. Neutralization: Acid + Base → Salt + Water. Types of salts: Normal (from strong acid/base), Acidic (excess acid). Preparing salts: action of acid on metal, insoluble base, or alkali. Solubility of salts in water is key to choosing the preparation method.
subject: Science
author: CBC Kenya Team
